tasks.short: Review the student's study progress, look up programme rules, advise on curricula and careers, and record the advice in the student file.

steps.what: Lecturer reviews the student's study progress across several screens
Lecturer looks up curricula and programme rules for the student
Lecturer advises students on academic and vocational curricula and career issues
Lecturer records the advice in the student file as free text

tasks.design: An advising view in the student records system ({OTHER}) shows credits earned, open requirements and fitting electives for the student's programme, computed from the programme rules, so the lecturer does not piece them together across screens and rule documents. Advice is recorded with a short template (topic, agreed next steps, referral). Advising stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Progress and rules were pieced together from several screens and documents.
tasks.enabler_now: Student records systems compute progress against programme rules.
tasks.still_hard: Exemptions and exchange credits are often missing.
tasks.human_edge: Helping a student see a career they had not thought of.

evidence.claim: Student records systems can compute progress against programme rules.
Student data processing needs a legal basis and minimal data.

assumptions: Boundary: from the advising request to advice recorded; formal exemptions are outside.
Input contract: programme rules coded; fallback is rule documents.
research_questions: Is preparation time per session shorter?

incremental.description: Lecturer reports wrong progress data to student administration.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: students with exemptions; high: standard programme students.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Teach live online classes, edit lecture recordings, check and upload them, answer forum questions, and follow up students who are inactive online.

steps.what: Lecturer teaches classes using online technology
Lecturer edits lecture recordings and adds chapters and captions by hand
Lecturer uploads the recording to the course page
Lecturer answers students' questions in the online forum
Lecturer checks who is inactive online and follows up

tasks.design: Lecture capture ({OTHER}) adds automatic captions and chapter marks to recordings, so the lecturer only trims and corrects them; once checked, the recording is released to the course page ({LMS}). Recurring questions are pinned in a course FAQ in the forum. A learning-system report lists students who have not logged in or submitted work, so the lecturer does not check each student. Teaching live stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Recordings were edited by hand, the same questions answered repeatedly and activity checked per student.
tasks.enabler_now: Lecture capture adds captions and chapters; learning systems report activity.
tasks.still_hard: Captions for literary quotations and names need correcting.
tasks.human_edge: Keeping an online group talking to each other.
tasks.altitude: The lecturer corrects instead of editing from scratch.

reach.learn: Whether recordings and answers arrive sooner.

evidence.claim: Lecture capture tools can add automatic captions and chapter marks; learning systems report student activity.
Emotion inference in education is banned; activity reports here count logins and submissions only.

assumptions: Boundary: from the online class to students followed up; grading is outside.
Input contract: lecture capture licensed; fallback is editing by hand.
Students read the FAQ before posting; a little student time is priced.
The lecturer checks every recording before release.

incremental.description: Students read the FAQ before asking.

approvals.approved_version: The recording as checked by the lecturer in s3.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: small groups with few questions; high: large online courses.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect lecturers' availability and course needs, build the course schedule, resolve clashes with colleagues, check the schedule, and send it to the timetabling office.

steps.what: Lecturer collects colleagues' availability and course needs by e-mail
Lecturer schedules courses in a spreadsheet
Lecturer checks the final course schedule
Lecturer e-mails the schedule to the timetabling office

tasks.design: Colleagues enter availability and course needs in a form in the timetabling tool ({OTHER}), so they are not collected by e-mail. The tool proposes a schedule from those inputs, room capacity and fixed rules (no clashes in a programme year, teaching-free days), and lists clashes it cannot solve. Once the lecturer has checked it, the schedule goes to the timetabling office in the tool. Resolving clashes with colleagues stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Needs were collected by e-mail and schedules built by hand in a spreadsheet.
tasks.enabler_now: Timetabling tools take availability forms and propose schedules by rules.
tasks.human_edge: Persuading a colleague to swap a slot.
tasks.altitude: The lecturer resolves conflicts instead of building the grid.

evidence.claim: Timetabling tools can collect availability by form and propose schedules from rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from next year's courses to the schedule sent; room booking is outside.
Input contract: colleagues fill the form; fallback is e-mail.
Colleagues spend a little time on the form; priced as other-role time.
research_questions: Do late changes to the schedule fall?

approvals.approved_version: The schedule as checked by the lecturer in s4.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many part-time staff; high: stable staff and rooms.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Meet colleagues on teaching and research issues, plan the meetings, write and share meeting notes, and co-write shared documents.

steps.what: Lecturer collaborates with colleagues in meetings on teaching and research issues
Lecturer plans meetings with colleagues by e-mail
Lecturer writes and shares meeting notes

loop.input: The recorded meeting, when every participant consents.
loop.output: Draft notes with decisions and actions.
loop.check: Every action must name an owner who was in the meeting; the lecturer edits the notes before sharing.
loop.stop: One draft per meeting; if anyone declines recording, the lecturer writes the notes.
loop.why_not_simpler: Discussions are free-form; a form does not capture them.

steps.what: Lecturer co-writes documents by e-mailing versions to colleagues

tasks.design: Meetings are planned with a shared-calendar poll ({CALENDAR}) instead of e-mail rounds. When all participants consent, a transcription tool drafts notes with decisions and actions, and the lecturer edits them before sharing. Shared documents are written together in one online file ({DOCS}) instead of e-mailed versions. Discussing issues with colleagues stays with the lecturer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Meetings were planned by e-mail, notes typed afterwards and versions mailed around.
tasks.enabler_now: Calendar polls, meeting transcription and shared editing are standard.
tasks.human_edge: Finding common ground between colleagues who disagree.

reach.learn: Whether notes and documents are current.

evidence.claim: Meeting tools can transcribe recordings and draft notes; shared editing replaces mailed versions.
Systems able to monitor staff need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from the shared issue to the document written; decisions by the department are outside.
Input contract: consent for recording; fallback is own notes.
Works council consent comes before recording.
research_questions: How much of the drafted notes is changed?

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few recorded meetings; high: frequent project meetings.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The lecturer keeps advising, teaching online, resolving schedule conflicts and working with colleagues; screen searching, recording edits, schedule building and note typing shrink.
skills_to_grow: Using lecture capture and timetabling tools
role.ambitious_version: A lecturer with more time for teaching and research.

job.title: English Language and Literature Teachers, Postsecondary
